story_text.value:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl

title.value: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share

story_text.value:
Since it was released Opus 5.5 has solved almost all the problems I've had with previous Anthropic models over the last year. On medium thinking level (default in Claude code) it's been remarkably more succinct and really good at understanding my questions and even anticipating my needs. Has been a markedly huge improvement over previous models and even had me commenting to a colleague the other day that if all advancement were to stop, it would be a useful tool for at least the next 5 years.

But over the last 2-3 days, it's started exhibiting some of the problems previous models presented. It's been making absurd assumptions without asking about my preferences. More definitively, in 3 instances I've had to either correct it on previous decisions that were made but it ignored. 2 times I've had to double check it on some quite obvious high level performance choices I've come to anticipate the model already understanding from prior experience, especially in the same project. At least twice I've had to call it out only get the remedial "you're totally right I should have done X instead".

Also to be clear, I'm not playing around with more advanced expensive models that fall back. This is all experience within a Pro plan using Opus 5.5 medium.

Anyone else been encountering weirdness?

title.value: Has Opus 5.5 gotten dumber for anyone else in the last few days?

story_text.value:
Hey HN!

I shared Optio here back in March. Originally it was focused on getting swarms of coding agents (claude code/codex) to drive PRs towards a merge by automatically resuming them on CI failures or PR comments.

Since then, I've reworked the project to be a general platform for running any kind of AI workflow on your infra by allowing users to configure each component of a possible workflow:

When: On demand, a cron schedule, or triggered by external events such as a webhook, slack message, ticket (jira/linear/gh), pagerduty/datadog/alertsmanager/pylon/sentry.

Where: In a k8s pod or any machine you have installed the optio daemon on (I use my laptop).

Who: Any harness you prefer (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, etc.)

What/Why: You can format parameters from the triggers directly into the prompts and then configure if the agent should exit, be resumed automatically, or be persistent.

You can either define workflows in the web ui or as yaml files that get synced to the orchestrator (ai config-as-code).

I've also built native iOS and Android apps so you can connect to your cluster and create/manage agents remotely.

The marketing page is at https://optio.host and the code is still open source at https://github.com/jonwiggins/optio

Would love feedback or any thoughts you might have on how I could make it better!

story_text.value:
Hey HN! As an avid user of cmux (https://cmux.com/), I wanted a way to control terminal and agent sessions from my Android phone, so I built Muxer. The app talks to a tiny relay over HTTPS, that then talks to cmux through its local socket, and gives you to ability to:

  - Answer agent permission requests, questions and plans from a notification
  - Reply to Claude Code, Codex and Pi chat sessions with text, voice, @ file mentions and photos
  - Receive all cmux notification, with inline replies, bubbles and background delivery.
  - Use a live terminal with sticky modifier keys and local scrollback
  - Share text and links from any app to an agent
  - Organize workspaces
  - Manage cmux Cloud VMs and automations
  - Lock the app with your fingerprint, face or screen lock
Enjoy, and let me know what you think!

story_text.value:
I'm an engineer, but I also hate using tools that make things overcomplicated.

It's also tough with the new pace of AI-driven development to really get into the flow state, and maintain (still needed!) focus on 1 thing.

So I built a tool that I actually want to use every day.

Curious if others would find this useful, too, or have any feedback? Like if it's nearly there, what changes would make this a win for your workflow?

Details:

- It's a Mac app (Apple Silicon) that runs your Claude Code sessions side by side. Each piece of work gets a "context" with its own session, next steps, status, PRs, and links.

- The dashboard groups contexts by whose move it is: yours, waiting on a reviewer or teammate, Claude working, or idle. You get a notification when a session needs you or a PR gets review comments.

- For non-engineers, there's a Chat view instead of the terminal, a guided Claude Code install, and folder pickers instead of paths. Engineers can stay in the real Claude Code terminal.

- It runs the actual claude CLI, and sessions keep running if you quit Perch. You can also import your existing Claude Code sessions.

- Everything stays on your Mac. There's no account and no analytics, and crash reports are opt-in.

title.value: Show HN: Perch, a calm Mac app for juggling Claude Code sessions

story_text.value:
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.

I ran two tasks on small repositories:

1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database. 2. Analyze a website's codebase.

Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.

I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:

- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens - Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens - Output: 39,324 tokens - Total: 1.59M tokens

At Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.

The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."

For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours using Opus 5.5 xhigh, mostly cached input. That's not a controlled benchmark, but the difference in usable capacity is staggering.

Both Kimi tasks failed without delivering results. I have video evidence and detailed logs, but won't publish private repository data.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSr-DLn88AM

Is this a quota-accounting bug, or are Kimi's $19 subscription limits intentionally this restrictive?

Disclosure: I also develop a competing coding agent. These tests used Kimi's official CLI.

title.value: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage

story_text.value:
The fastest way to learn harness engineering? Build Claude Code from scratch.

Why harness engineering? LangChain kept the same model and changed only the harness. Their coding agent went from 53% to 67% on Terminal-Bench, a top coding-agent benchmark. From outside the top 30 to the top 5. Same model. Better harness.

Over the past few months, I've taken apart Claude Code, OpenCode, and Pi to see how they work under the hood.

And you don't need to ship a coding agent for this to pay off. The same foundations power any agent, in e-commerce, finance, or sales.

On top of that, people are increasingly realizing they need to build their own harness instead of relying on Claude Code or Codex. Ramp scaling its operations with a custom harness is a perfect example.

So I turned what I learned into an in-depth course on harness engineering by building Claude Code from scratch. It's free and open source: 8 articles, 6 videos, and one codebase. It's perfect for people who learn by building. Everything in Python.

For full transparency, Modal, Opik, and Kitaru sponsor the course, which lets me keep it 100% free as an independent AI engineer.

Here are the 8 steps that I think are core to building and maintaining any harness:

1. Design the harness 2. Build the bare-bones agent loop 3. Sandbox it, locally and remotely 4. Apply 4 essential context engineering techniques 5. Add subagents as a context engineering technique 6. Deploy it headless to the cloud: CLI, webhooks, cron 7. Build benchmarks to measure it 8. Replay failed runs to debug agents

Everything is on GitHub: https://github.com/decodingai-magazine/building-a-coding-agent-from-scratch-course

Curious what others here think. Which of these steps has been the hardest to get right in your own agents?

story_text.value:
I'm building Multipeer, a desktop app for running agents, tools and working wth teammates on one shared canvas.

I often have several agent sessions open at once, but they're all scattered across terminals. It was also hard for my co-founder to see what my agents are doing or jump in to work together. So We built the solution to our own problem. And now we're releasing it to the world.

It's a macOS app for now (soon on Windows and Linux). You can invite your teammates over a local network or over the internet. They can follow your view and, if you allow them, they can also take control of your terminal and claude code/codex sessions.

The app is still early, and I'm also releasing the iPhone/Android app soon to remotely control everything on your canvas.

I'd would like to get feedback from the HN community! If there's any features you'd like to see, please contact me via: shyam@multipeer.sh, we build really fast. I'd love to talk to everyone of you and work on your feedback!

Thanks!
